Surah Al-Layl (The Night)

Meccan, and its verses number twenty-one.

﴿By the night when it covers﴾, i.e., when it covers the sun, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿By the night when it covers it﴾. Or [it covers] the day, or everything that it conceals with its darkness.
﴿By the day when it reveals itself﴾ means it appears when the darkness of the night departs, or it becomes clear and unveiled with the rising of the sun.

﴿And He who created the male and the female﴾. That is: and by the Mighty, the One of great power, who created the two kinds, male and female, among every creature that has offspring. It was also said that they are Adam and Eve. It was recited as "وَالذَّكَرِ وَالْأُنْثَى" (wal-dhakari wal-unthā), and it was recited as "وَالَّذِي خَلَقَ الذَّكَرَ وَالْأُنْثَى" (wal-ladhī khalaqa al-dhakara wal-unthā). It was also said that "مَا" (mā) is maṣdariyyah (a verbal-noun particle, forming a verbal noun from the verb that follows it).

Qur'an 92:4: ﴿Indeed, your efforts are diverse.﴾ It is the answer to the oath (jawab al-qasam), and "shatta" (scattered, divergent) is the plural of "shatit," meaning: indeed, your endeavors are of varied and divergent kinds.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 92, verses 5–6:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿As for him who gives and fears [Allah]﴾ ﴿and believes in the best [reward]﴾ ... etc., is a detailed explanation of those scattered endeavors and a clarification of their rulings. That is: as for him who gives the rights of his wealth, and fears Allah Exalted by avoiding His prohibitions which He has forbidden, and believes in the best attribute (al-khaṣla al-ḥusnā), which is faith (al-īmān); or in the best word, which is the word of tawhid (kalimat al-tawḥīd); or in the best religion (al-milla al-ḥusnā), which is the religion of Islam; or in the best reward (al-mathūba al-ḥusnā), which is Paradise.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 92, verses 5–6:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿As for him who gives and fears [Allah]﴾ ﴿and believes in the best [reward]﴾ ... etc., is a detailed explanation of those scattered endeavors and a clarification of their rulings. That is: as for him who gives the rights of his wealth, and fears Allah Exalted by avoiding His prohibitions which He has forbidden, and believes in the best attribute (al-khaṣla al-ḥusnā), which is faith (al-īmān); or in the best word, which is the word of tawhid (kalimat al-tawḥīd); or in the best religion (al-milla al-ḥusnā), which is the religion of Islam; or in the best reward (al-mathūba al-ḥusnā), which is Paradise.

"So We will ease him toward ease" — ﴿So We will ease him toward ease﴾. Then We will prepare him for the disposition that leads to ease and comfort, such as entering Paradise and its beginnings, from the expression (yassara al-faras lil-rukub, "he made the horse ready for riding"): when he saddles it and bridles it.

ALL of the verse 92:8 excerpt is needed. Translating:

﴿But as for he who is niggardly﴾, that is, with his wealth, not spending it in the way of good. (p-167) ﴿and considers himself self-sufficient﴾, that is, he renounces what is with Allah, the Exalted, as though he were independent of it, so he does not fear Him; or he is self-sufficient through the desires of this world, (and so) dispenses with the bliss of the Hereafter.

Translation:

﴿And denied the best﴾ — i.e., what was mentioned of the interrelated meanings.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 92, verse 10:

﴿So We shall ease him toward the hardship﴾. That is: toward the course that leads to hardship and severity, such as entering the Fire and its preliminaries, because of his choosing it. Perhaps the reason the two divisions are introduced with giving and stinginess, although each of them is of lower rank than what follows them in bringing about facilitation toward ease (al-yusra) and facilitation toward hardship (al-'usra), is to indicate that each of them is a root in what has been mentioned, not a completion of what follows them of affirmation (al-tasdiq), piety (al-taqwa), denial (al-takdhib) and self-sufficiency (al-istighna'). The explanation of the first as giving obedience, and of the second as stinginess with what he is commanded, although it is contrary to the apparent meaning, is rejected by His statement, may He be exalted: *

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 92, verse 11:

﴿And his wealth will not avail him﴾ meaning: and it will not avail him, or "what will avail him" [i.e., the interrogative is taken as a negation], ﴿his wealth﴾ which he withholds stingily with, ﴿when he falls [tara daa]﴾ meaning: he perishes. "Taraddā" is of the form "tafa''ala" from al-radā (tafsir: the perdition), which is destruction (al-halak); or he falls into the pit when he is buried, or he falls into the depths of Jahannam.

Verse 12 of Surah 92: ﴿Indeed, upon Us is guidance.﴾ This is a resumptive clause (istitnaf) that confirms what precedes it. That is: indeed, it is incumbent upon Us, in accordance with Our decree, which is founded upon far-reaching wisdom, that since We created creation for worship, We make clear to them the path of guidance, and the path of error and what leads to it. And We have done this completely, leaving nothing further to add, since We have explained the condition of whoever takes either of the two paths, by way of encouragement and warning. From here it becomes clear that guidance (al-hidayah, i.e. showing the way) is the indication toward what leads to the desired goal, not the indication that necessarily brings one to it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 92, verse 13:

﴿And indeed, to Us belong the Hereafter and the first life.﴾ That is: the complete disposal of both, as We wish, so We act within them with whatever actions We will, among which is what We have promised of facilitating the path to ease (al-yusra) and facilitating the path to hardship (al-'usra). It was also said: indeed, to Us belongs everything in this world and the Hereafter, so your refusal to seek guidance by Our guidance does not harm Us.
﴿فَأنْذَرْتُكم نارًا تَلَظّى﴾ By omitting one of the two تَاءَيْنِ from تَتَلَظّى, i.e., تَتَلَهَّبُ (it blazes). It is also read in its original form.

﴿Only the most wretched will burn in it﴾ — meaning, will burn in it perpetually (ṣiliyyan lāziman).

﴿Except the most wretched﴾ — meaning, except the disbeliever (al-kāfir). For the sinner (al-fāsiq) will not burn in it perpetually, and this has been made explicit by the words of the Exalted: *

"Who denies and turns away" — that is, he denied the truth and turned away from obedience.

Note: the verse is ﴿الَّذِي كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ﴾ (92:16), rendered above as "Who denies and turns away."

(p-168) ﴿And the most pious will be kept far from it﴾: that is, he will be removed far from it, ﴿the most pious﴾, the one who exerts himself to the utmost in guarding against disbelief (kufr) and sins (ma'asi). So he will not even come near it, let alone enter it or burn in it eternally. As for one who is below him, of those who guard against disbelief but not against sins, he will not be removed from it to this degree. This does not entail burning in it in the sense mentioned, so it does not contradict the preceding restriction (hasr).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 92, verse 18:

﴿The one who gives his wealth﴾ gives it and spends it in the ways of righteousness and good deeds. And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿seeking to purify himself﴾ is either a substitute (badal) for "yu'ti" and falls within the sphere of the relative clause (silah), having no place in i'rab; or it lies in the place of the accusative (nasb), being a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "yu'ti," meaning: he seeks that he be, in the sight of Allah exalted is He, one who purifies and increases, not intending thereby ostentation (riya') or reputation (sum'ah).

Qur'anic verse: ﴿And there is not for anyone with Him any favor that is repaid,﴾

This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf muqarrir) confirming that his giving of his wealth for purification (li-al-tazakki) is sincerely for the sake of God, the Exalted. That is: there is no one who has with Him a favor of a kind that is to be repaid or compensated, so that he would intend, by giving what he gives, its recompense.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Except seeking the Face of his Lord, the Most High﴾ is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati', an exception that is not of the same category as what precedes it) from "نِعْمَةٍ" (ni'mah, "a favour"). It has also been read in the nominative (marfu') as a substitute (badal) for the grammatical position of "نِعْمَةٍ", since the position is nominative. The nominative may be either as the agent (fa'iliyyah) or as the subject of a nominal sentence (ibtida'), and "مِن" (min) is redundant (mazidah). It is also permissible for it to be an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), because the meaning is: he gives his wealth only seeking the Face of his Lord, not as a repayment for a favour.

The verses were revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, when he bought Bilal and a group of others whom the polytheists were harming, and he freed them. For this reason they said: the intended one of "the most wretched" (al-ashqa) is Abu Jahl or Umayya ibn Khalaf. 'Ata' and al-Dahhak have narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the polytheists tortured Bilal, and Bilal was saying: "One, One." The Prophet (ﷺ) passed by him and said: "One," meaning: Allah, Exalted is He, will save you. Then he said to Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him: "Indeed Bilal is being tortured for the sake of Allah." Abu Bakr understood what he (ﷺ) intended, so he went to his house, took a ratl of gold, and proceeded with it to Umayya ibn Khalaf, and said to him: "Will you sell Bilal to me?" He said: "Yes." So he bought him and freed him. The polytheists said: "Abu Bakr only freed him because of a favour he had owed him." So it was revealed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 92, verse 21:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He will surely be well-pleased﴾ is the answer to an implied oath, meaning: "By Allah, He will surely be well-pleased." It is a generous promise of attaining everything one seeks, in the most complete and most beautiful manner, since contentment (ridha) is realized through it. It has also been read as "yurda" (passive voice), from the causative (al-irda', "to cause to be pleased").

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Layl, Allah will give him until he is pleased, and will protect him from hardship and make ease easy for him."
